subtopic: LORD STRATHCONA- GIFT TO THE DOMINION.
LORD STRATHCONA- GIFT TO THE DOMINION.
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called, I would like to bring before the House a matter of considerable importance. A few days ago, when the militia estimates were under discussion I had the honour of bringing to the attention of the Committee of the Whole a branch of the subject which I considered of great interest to this country. In doing so, I used the following words :
On several occasions in this House I have had the honour to bring up this matter, and to say I hope the time will come when, in all the schools of Canada, there will be undertaken by the respective provincial governments, which of course control education, n uniform system of physical training for younger children, of elementary drill for the older ones, and of rifle shooting for those still older. I am happy to say that this policy if it may be dignified by that name, has been very generally discussed throughout the Do-mmion; and so far as I have observed, all the. best newspapers which more correctly indicate the trend of public opinion, have favoured this idea almost without exception.
I went on to say that I had reason to believe that all the provinces throughout the Dominion would follow the example set by the province of Nova Scotia and enter into an arrangement with the Dominion government by which this system of physical training and elementary drill in the schools might be carried out by mutual co-oneration between the Dominion government and the provinces. Yesterday I had the honour to receive from Lord Strath-cona-an old friend of Canada, who delights to call Canada his home, and who has on frequent occasions shown his deep interest in the development of this country -a letteT which I shall read to the House, as it expresses his own views better than any language of mine could do :
28 Grosvenor Square,
13th March, 1909.
My dear Sir Frederick Borden,-You will recollect that, when we met in London during your recent visit, I was greatly interested in the account you gave me of your efforts to get a system of physical training and military drill, including rifle practice, introduced into the public schools of the Dominion.
I have long entertained the opinion that such training as that you are striving for is of the highest value in developing the moral, physical and intellectual qualities of children, as well as that valuable quality known as patriotism), and I am anxious to take part in the good work which is being done in this direction.
I write, therefore, to inform you that I am prepared to place at your disposal, or that of

any competent body which you may be in a position to constitute, with the object ot encouraging such training, the sum of 5)10,000 per annum. I would suggest that the fund which this sum would form might be designated as for ' The encouragement of Physical and Military Training in Public Schools, and that it should be administered by a body of trustees appointed for the purpose. I should be glad to know what your own proposals as to the constitution of this body would be, but 1 think that the central committee might perhaps be composed somewhat as follows: xqurtell or the Minister of Militia for the time being, as president; the ministers who deal with education in the various provinces of the Dominion as vice- presidents, but subject to the conditions that the province which each one represents has declared its adhesion to the principles agreed upon between the Department of Militia and the province of Nova Scotia, which were sanctioned and made applicable to the other provinces of the Dominion by the orders in council of 13th August, 1908; the executive council to be composed of (a) the members of the Militia Council; (b) representatives to be named by the ministers controlling education in the various provinces -two each for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and one each for the remaining provinces of the Dominion; (c) the military officers commanding the commands and independent districts of the Dominion. Should His Excellency the Governor General be disposed to become patron of the trust, I should feel especially honoured by such action on his part, which would conduce very greatly to the success of the object which we have in view.
I should also deem it an especial honour it tiie Prime Minister, as evincing his approval, would consent to be vice-patron of the trust.
While the fund as a whole should be administered and money grants allotted by the executive committee-an general, proportionately to the school population of the various provinces of the Dominion-it would, I think, be desirable that the administration of the grant within the several provinces should be made by local committees, appointed under the authority of the central committee. These local committees might be composed, for example, of the military officer commanding the district, as chairman; three civil members, nominated by the Minister of Education for the province, and three military members, nominated by the Minister of Militia.
While I attach the highest importance to the advantages of physical training and elementary drill for all children of both sexes, I am particularly anxious that the especial value of military drill, including rifle shooting for boys capable of using rifles, should be constantly borne in mind. My object is not only to help to improve the physical and intellectual capabilities of the children by inculcating habits of alertness, orderliness and prompt obedience, but also to bring up the boys to patriotism and to a realization that the first duty of a free citizen is to be prepared to defend liis country. The Dominion at the present time, and for many years to come, can hardly hope to be able to give so long a period of training to her military forces as by itself would suffice to make them efficient soldiers, but, if all boys had acquired a fair acquaintance while at school with Sir FREDERICK BORDEN.
simple military drill and rifle shooting, the degree of efficiency which could be reached in the otherwise short period which can be devoted to the military training of the Dominion forces would, in my opinion, be enormously enhanced.
I will only add that I should prefer that, for the present at least, the whole of the money grant should be devoted to those educational establishments which are maintained entirely out of public funds. I think, further, that the administration of the fund should be such as to enable both sexes, whether teachers or pupils, to share in the rewards, and that the allotments o'f money should be so made as to afford an inducement both to the teachers to instruct and to the pupils to perfect themselves in the training desired.
Believe me to be,
My dear Sir Frederick,
Very truly yours,

In reply to this letter, I at once caused the following telegram to be sent:
Ottawa, 23rd March, 1909. Strathcona, London.
Your letter 13th received. Gratefully ac-c.ept your most generous offer to create fund for the encouragement of physical and military training in public schools of Canada. Organization outlined in your letter appears admirably adapted to attain end in view. Am forwarding by mail detailed proposals based thereon for carrying out the scheme. Hope you will consent to fund being called the Strathcona Trust for the encouragement of physical and military training in publio schools. His Excellency the Governor General accepts position of patron and the Premier consents to become vice-patron.

I may say, in addition that I received from His Excellency his consent to notify Lord Strathcona that he would accept the position of patron. The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is here to speak for himself. He has already informed me that he will gladly accept the position of vicepatron.	.
In a private letter, Lord Strathcona informs me that, on hearing from me a cheque for $250,000 will be forwarded as the basis of the fund to provide the annual income of $10,000. I thought this matter to be of sufficient importance to justify me in bringing it up in this way.

I believe I shall voice the sentiments of this House, if, without losing a moment, I move that we offer our thanks to Lord Strathcona for the letter which has just been communicated to the House by the Minister of Militia. Lord Strathcona has rendered many services^ to Canada, but, I believe, none of greater importance than the present one. Physical education is of the greatest possible importance, and its value has never, in the history of the world, been understood as it

is now. I hope and firmly believe, that the system now initiated by Lord Strath-eona, the organization which he sets on foot, will provide that, in all parts of Canada, physical training will become part of the education of the boys and girls of this country. I beg leave to move, seconded by Mr. R. L. Borden:
That the thanks of the House of Commons and the people of Canada are hereby tendered to Lord St rath eon a for his letter to the Minister of Militia just communicated to the House.

I have the very greatest pleasure in seconding the motion which the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has just proposed to the House. Lord Strathcona's offer will be received with feelings of the deepest appreciation, not only by members of this House regardless of party, but by all patriotic citizens regardless of party. This act of Lord Strathcona's is entirely in harmony with the many patriotic actions which have distinguished his wonderful career. His encouragement of physical training andi of elementary drill amongst the children of the country is a most worthy object. I have no doubt whatever that this most worthy object will be stimulated to a very great degree by the foundation of this fund. I am sure that all of us earnestly hope and sincerely believe that it will be productive of all the great benefits and advantages to the people of this country which are so eloquently set forth in this letter with which Lord Strathcona has accompanied his gift.
Motion agreed to.

Has his attention been called to the artistic work being done in the vicinity of the front entrance to the pathway up to the buildings?

Ottawa public buildings-heating, including salaries of engineers, firemen and watchmen- additional amount, $10,000.

No.

We pay a flat rate of $2.25 per lamp up to three thousand lamps, and $2 over that.
What is a lamp?
Sixteen candle power.
How do you get at that basis?
After investigation of the charges ordinarily made by electric companies. I think the rate is a reasonable one. We have about 1(>,000 lights altogether.
Has the minister paid any personal attention to the distribution of lights? Is it possible we are uneconomical in the number used?

I had occasion to inquire into the considerations which led us to make the present arrangement, and satisfy myself that the arrangement was a reasonable one. The details, of course, we must leave to our electricians, who are faithful and responsible men.
Who is the head of the service?
Mr. Johnston is the chief electrician.
Does he see to it that useless lights are not used?
Yes, he reports on every application for lights.
How many lights are kept burning on the average?
It would be difficult to tell that; lights burned in an office to-day would not be burned to-morrow.

When the winter is over,
I suppose that many lamps are not used all summer long. Is $2.25 paid for every lamp that swings?
Yes. Of course, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) will understand that if a lamp were kept burning winter and summer on a meter rate, it would cost much more than $2 a year.

It would be interesting to know how many lamps are burned eight hours a day, how many six hours a day and so on. It must be that many of thern do not cost much to the contractor. Possibly you may be paying a very high rate for the light you are consuming.
It is a matter for careful calculation by the electrician. I have no doubt that the matter was very carefully gone into when the arrangement was made.

It is possible that, having made your contract, the thing is considered done-you are going it- blind, as it were. But it seems to me that a man, if this were his own business, would have somebody keep pretty sharp tab on it all to find out, as nearly as he could, the power he was Mr. PUGSLET.
using, and he would revise his contract if he thought he was paying too much. Of course, he might find that he was not paying too much, and so let it run. Is the minister taking any means of checking this business, so as to have information for his own guidance and for the use of this committee? If not, I would advise him to ask his officers-he has plenty of them; some are overworked, but some are not, and he could easily choose those who would not be overburdened with the duty-_ to make adequate investigation of this business and furnish him with information, which, I am sure, he would like to have and which, possibly, the House may ask for.

I am told that there i9 a report. There is no doubt that it would be an advantage to have the electrician go into the matter carefully from time to time and see how we are faring. I will have the report brought down and laid on the table at a convenient time.

()thiwa public buildings-telephone service -additional amount, $2,850.
I would like some information about the system on which telephones are furnished.
Local Manager.
When was the $35 arrangement entered into?
About 15 or 20 years ago.

What diminution in the
price of the house and office phones has taken place in the city within that time?
I do not think there has been any diminution.
Does the minister know what the rate is with reference to a longer contract than one year? That letter mentions a yearly contract.
I think there is no difference in the rate.
He specifically mentions a contract for a year.
He says the government can terminate at any time, while an ordinary customer must pay by the year.

I have an impression that
the rates for the city in the last 15 years have diminished-the minister can easily get the information. But if that be true, there ought to be an equitable and proportional diminution in the $35 rate. The company was doing business with an excellent customer, to whom they now furnish over 300 phones. If, 15 years ago, they gave that as a fair rate, and if at that time business and residence phones were higher in the city, it is only fair that they should make a proportional reduction in the present rate. The minister might look into that and see. Any way, the government is an excellent and very large cus-

tomer, there is no competition in the business, and I think the company should take the general rule of business into account that the larger the customer the greater the consideration they show in the wares they have to sell. On the other hand, what is the rule upon which these phones are distributed? There are a great many of them, and I have information which leads me to think that there are a good many which can hardly be justified. What jiass of officials get phones?

Answering my hon. friend's first remark, I will make inquiry as to whether there has been any change in the rates. But to-day, taking business phones at $45 and residence phones at $25, if we paid that rate, we would be paying $1,600 per year more than we do at present on the $35 rate all round.
My point was in regard to the proportional diminution if there has been any.

In regard to our getting a reduced rate because we are having a good many telephones, I doubt very much if we could get the telephone company to do that, because private individuals would at once complain. They would say:	You
are only charging the government a certain rate per year and you are charging us $5 or $10 per year more as the case might be.
They might say that now.
No, they cannot say that now because it is a flat rate that we pay for offices and residences.
You said that you got them for $1,600 less?
Yes, that may be.
You are getting a compromise rate between the residence and office rate?

Yes. I might say something as to the reasons for installing these telephones. It goes without saying that telephones will be put into the offices of the ministers, the deputy ministers and the various officials wlio would be required to be communicated with by telephone. I suppose that the hon. gentleman would rather have me say a word as to residence telephones?
Yes, as to whether the number is required.

We do not install a telephone in any office unless there is a requisition endorsed by the minister of the department. I am asking in all cases that a requisition from any department shall be in the form of a request from the minister for a telephone. I think that is only right. The minister would know whether Mr. FOSTER.
it is reasonable that there should be a telephone placed in such and such an office, and he endorses his approval on the requisition. With regard to residences, it is the same way. We have telephones in the residences of the ministers, of tihe deputy ministers, of the chief officials of the departments, of the secretaries of the departments, and in some cases of one of the messengers of a department. We have thought it was not unreasonable to put a telephone in the residene of the chief messenger who might be called up from time to time by his minister or some one connected with the department. I think, m a general way, that is the principle upon which we have gone.
Is there only one messenger's telephone?
I do not know whether there is more than one messenger in the department who has a telephone in his residence.
You mean the chief messenger in each department?
Not the chief messenger, but the messenger who might be chosen by the minister.
One from each department?
They do not all have them. It is only in very rare cases that there are telephones in the messenger s residence. I have a list which I will send over to the hon. gentleman.
It was claimed that the government pay as high as $50 for some telephones.
A desk extension is $15 additional.
Is the minister sure that in some of the rooms they do not have three telephones where one may do?

I cannot think that is the case. I have had no such case brought to my notice, and in looking over the list it would not appear that such is the case. I may say that I have had requests for telephones which I have refused.
I have no doubt of that.
I see a good many telephones in the Public Works Department down at $55 apiece.

There might be two extensions. There is a desk telephone in my own office and a desk telephone and an extension would make $55.
Rideau Hall, including grounds-improvements, furniture and maintenance-additional amount, $4,000.

That will make the total nearly $39,000.
Any extraordinary improvements included in that?
No.
Any addition or improvements to Government house itself?
No, just the grounds.
No new furniture?

Yes, there would be some dry goods, linen, curtains and glassware, but the main part of it was for improvements and maintenance. The principal part of it is for salaries, $17,000; that would be for general work about the grounds. Then we paid a little over $7,500 for dry goods, linen, curtains, glassware, crockery and kitchen ware, $1,396 for lumber, $842 for furniture, flags, and cleaning carpets and $1,698 for plants, bulbs, trees, &c.
$17,000 for labour?
Yes.
For taking care of the grounds?

For taking care of the grounds, including the salary of clerk of works, the conservatories, &c.
Dominion public buildings-heating-additional amount, $23,000.

The expenditure from April 1 to December 15, 1908, was $79,500. There are contracts for coal not paid, amounting to $33,500, making a total of $113,000. There was a vote in the estimates last year of $90,000, leaving a balance of $23,000 which we are now asking for?
Arisaig harbour-repairs to wharf and breakwater, $500.
What is the nature of that item?

This is to complete the payments according to the pay-lists and accounts not covered in the vote of $1,500 in the main estimates. I had that reduced 102
to $1,100, stating that we would make a payment out of supplementaries for the current year.
Bailey's Brook-harbour improvements, $700.
This is a balance. It is for reconstructing and extending the brush-work on the east side of the harbour.
Does that complete the contemplated improvements?

Yes, it will complete the present extension.
Glace Bay harbour-assistance towards harbour improvements, $900.

This is to pay the balance.
Grand Etang-partial reconstruction of channel protection works, $3,300.
Mr. PUGSLEY I gave the particulars of this the other night to the hon. member for St. Antoine Division.
Little River harbour wharf-additional amount, $200.
This is to close up the year.
Is this in Digby?
It is in Yarmouth.
There is a Little River in Digby for which $2,500 was in the estimate last year.
That is not here.
Was that omitted from tjie estimates because Digby returned a Conservative instead of a Liberal?
What does the hon. gentleman himself think?
I am not replying to but asking questions.
It is your thinker he wants to work.
I have not thought of that at all.

It is a question of extreme delicacy.
Portuguese Cove breakwater-strengthening structure, $2,000.

This is to cover overexpenditure, to finish up the payments.
Scotch Cove (White Point)-breakwater-to complete payments, $9,350.
What is the total expenditure on that?

The total expenditure up to the first of January was $20,274. This amount is due the contractor. The contract is for $28,935.



South Lake, Lakevale-opening channel from lake to St. George's bay-inclusive of protection work-additional amount, $4,500.
I gave the full particulars of that to Mr. Ames the other night.
This work was undertaken before the money was provided?

This is a case in which, owing to an error, the amount was reduced, but it was found to be absolutely necessary work in order to protect what had already been done. The engineer went on and finished it and this is the balance.
Upper Prospect-breakwater, $250.
Where is this?
This is in Halifax county.
Is this to complete the work?

This is to complete the payments, yes.
Sandy Cove breakwater-to provide for full and final settlement of outstanding accounts for labour and materials supplied in connection with construction of breakwater in 1903-4 by contractors Hayden & Oliver, $3,945.

This is a case which I think I should explain to the committee. The contractors took the contract to build this breakwater. The report of the engineer is that after they had proceeded a certain distance with the work it was discovered that the soil was entirely different from what the engineer and contractors had expected it would be. The result of placing the foundation of the breakwater there was to give a certain direction to the current which began to undermine the foundation. When this was discovered, the contractors saw that to go on with the work meant inevitable loss to them and they were of the opinion that they had better forfeit their deposit and abandon their contract. The engineer encouraged them to go ahead with the work and finish it up and stated to them that he would so report to the department and ask favourable consideration. The contractors say that they understood from the engineer that he would recommend that they should be paid the actual cost of the work. He does not recollect that that took place, but he does recollect that he encouraged them to proceed with the work and does not deny that he led them to expect that the department would be likely to take an equitable view of the case. They went on and built the breakwater, doing a thoroughly good job, which is very satisfactory to the department. The result of doing the work was to bankrupt the contractors. Then the men who had done work upon the breakwater and people who had supplied1

materials made a claim upon the department urging that as the government had got full value for what was represented by the actual labour and materials, the government ought not to allow these men to lose their wages or the value of the material supplied.
When did they make their claim?

At least two years ago. The department sent an accountant in November, 1906, down to the place where the work had been done to look into these bills for wages and materials, and the accountant certified that this amount was justly due. The engineer certified that there is no question whatever but that the actual cost of the work would be represented by this balance of $3,945.08, and we have the claims actually filed with us to that amount.
What was the total amount of the contract?

$12,900, but the actual cost of the work was that amount plus this $3,945. The matter came before me at the last session and I declined to recommend this claim because I felt it was establishing a precedent which might lead us into difficulties in the future, that the contractors had taken the work as being the lowest tenderers at the contract price of $12,900, that the men who did the work and supplied the materials trusted to the contractors, and that therefore, if the contractors were unable to pay, they would have to lose what they had put into the work. I declined to bring it before the House at the last session of parliament. Since that time the matter has been still further urged upon my attention, and I looked again into the report of the engineer, and I concluded that, in view of the fact that the work was honestly done and thoroughly done, if we do not pay, it means that these poor men who have worked on this public work will lose the fruit of their labour, and the men who supplied the materials will lose the price of them; and also, in view of the fact that the contractor was going to throw up his job when he encountered this unexpected condition of affairs, and was pursuaded by the engineer to go on and complete the contract with the expectation-not a very strong one, I admit-[DOT] that the department would look on the matter equitably, I concluded that it was not unreasonable to ask parliament to vote this money, and I hope the committee will concur in that view.
To whom will the money be paid?

It will be paid to the men according to the claims filed in the department.

Dorchester wharf-addition, $5,500.

This is to build a very important extension of the wharf, some 200 feet long, 94 feet high on the average, and 52 feet wide on the top. It is a very important work; it is under contract, and this is to complete the payments.
What is the total cost?

$17,724.83. There is a great deal of business being done there, and it is increasing. This work was necessitated by reason of the business being largely done by steamers instead of by sailing vessels.
Who was the contractor?

Downey & Downey,of Curryville, New Brunswick.
Richibucto harbour-to pay John Jardine, contractor, in full and final settlement of all claims in connection with his contract of November 16, 1905, for extension of breakwater-pier on the north side of harbour, $5,395.34.
Are these extra amounts based on the schedule prices?
Yes, but the larger portion is at $1.25 per cubic yard, all the resident engineer would allow.
Was Mr. Jardine authorized or directed by any officer of the department to build this addition or extension after the letting of the contract?

No, he was not authorized to build the extension, and that is the reason the department could not pay for it, and that is why we come to parliament. It is a useful public work, and it is only right that the contractor should be paid for it.
Does the minister state that Mr. Jardine did this additional work without communicating with the department and getting the authority of the department to do it?
That is correct.
And then he presents a claim to the minister and asks for this extra payment?
Yes, if parliament approves.

That is pretty dangerous work.
St. John river and tributaries-construction of wharfs in tidal waters-additional amount, $4,650.
I understand that this amount, added to the amount already voted in the main estimates, makes $19,650 for the construction of wharfs in the St. John river for the year ending the 31st March, 1909.
Yes.

I understand there were four or five wharfs ordered to be built by the department last summer in the counties of Queens and Sunbury, and that without tender or contract. Can the minister tell us what is the position with regard to these wharfs? I would like to know what the total cost of each of these is to be.

At Chase's Point, $4,110; Oromocto, $4,379; Majorville high water wharf, $4,996; Gowan's, $2,750; Rothesay, $1,964; Long Island, $869; Meaford, $543.

Total, $19,611, and the appropriation was $15,000, leaving a balance of $4,011, and we are asking for $4,075.
Will this appropriation *complete all these wharfs?
These amounts are required to make the payments up to March 31, and I hope , they will complete these works, but am not sure.

I would like additional information with regard to a number of wharfs for which tenders were called during October last. The minister gave a list some days ago of nine wharfs for which tenders were called on October 9. In the call for tenders, November 12 was fixed as the last day when tenders would be received. I put a question on the Order Paper the other day, and was rather surprised, in view of what had transpired in Committee of Supply when the item of $20,000 was going through, at the amount of the estimated cost of these wharfs, as reported by the minister in reply to that question. 1 find that the estimated cost of the nine wharfs ran all the way from $4,861 to $19,561, and that the total estimated cost of the nine wharfs was $97,587. Those tenders were called, as the minister has informed us, upon plans and specifications prepared by the department on October 9, and the tenders were to be received up to November 12. Tenders were received for several of these wharfs, and notwithstanding the fact that in all cases they were considerably below the estimated cost, none of them were accepted. I would like the minister to explain why it was that his department, on October 9, just in the middle of an election campaign, called for tenders for the construction of so many wharfs in that constituency, and as soon as the election was over decided not to go on with the work. I would like to know also if it is the intention of the department during this year to call for new tenders for any of these wharfs?

The reason why tenders were called for before the election was because there was not time to call for them earlier. They were called for last fall and there was no particular reason why we should wait till after the elections.
The necessity arose very suddenly.

No, my hon. friend must be aware that while the estimates were submitted early last year, for reasons which, I suppose, our hon. friends opposite thought good and sufficient, they did not seem quite willing, for some time at all events, that the estimates should go through without considerable discussion, and, may I say it without offence, some little opposition. The result was we did not Mr. PUGSLEY.
get Supply until very shortly before prorogation. Parliament rose on July 20. I gave instructions immediately to have the plans and specifications prepared so that tenders could be invited. I did so because the information I had was that these wharfs were necessary in the public interest, and it would be desirable to have them put under way during the past winter. As soon as the plans were prepared by our engineer in St. John, Mr. Scammel, tenders were called for and in most cases they were somewhat below the estimates, but not very much below except in two instances. I had not myself gone carefully into the specifications, nor would I be supposed to do that, not being an engineer; but I did not anticipate that the plans would be very different from those which, when I was a member of the provincial government, we had prepared for wharfs constructed on the St. John river. When the tenders came in they struck me as very excessive. I could not conceive it possible that tenders would be called for wharfs that would cost so much beyond what the provincial government had succeeded in getting wharfs built for on the St. John river and its tributary lakes.
It arose from the condition of the political atmosphere at that particular time.

No, it arose by reason of the very different kind of plans which the engineer in my department at St. John had prepared, plans for a more substantial wharf-really a coast wharf instead of a river wharf.
Which showed good judgment on the part of the engineer.

I do not know. Some engineers are in favour of very substantia] wharfs, and it may be good economy in the long run; but at all events, I assumed that we would get a class of wharf similar to what the provincial government had been in the habit of building. There were two cases in which the tenders were very much less than the engineer's estimate, and I had these parties seen by one in whom I had confidence to ascertain if they really understood the plans and were prepared to to enter on the work. They said they had misunderstood the plans and could not possibly do the work at the price they [DOT] tendered, and I did not call on them to enter into contracts which would have ruined them. They were farmers from Queens and Sunbury. I decided to call for new tenders and ordered new plans to be prepared. I have communicated with the Chief Commissioner of Public Works in the New Brunswick government and have asked if he would allow me to have the benefit of the experience of his provincial engin-

eer who has had a great deal to do with the building of these wharfs, so that we might have plans prepared for wharfs of the same class as the provincial government is in the habit of building, and which run in cost from $1,000 to $2,000. He has consented, very kindly, to allow me to have the benefit of the experience and services of the engineer. I am going to have the engineer of my department in St. John, Mr. Cawmill, confer with him, and we expect to. get up a series of plans for the wharfs which will enable us to build a large number of these wharfs at a cost not to exceed the appropriation asked for in the main estimates. With regard to the different wharfs _ to which the 'hon. member has referred, it is my intention to call for tenders for these, unless it is pointed out to me that some of them are not necessary in the public interest. It may be that some information will come to me that will lead me to alter my opinion, but, as at present advised, I think they are all necessary in the public interest; and it is my hope-and my expectation also-that, during the coming season, the plans will be completed and tenders will be called for, I have the hope and expectation that the cost will not exceed from $1,000 to $2,000 for each wharf. I think we can get wharfs suitable for the St. John river and tributary lakes which will answer every purpose at a cost not to exceed on the average $2,000.

And the $20,000 voted will completely cover the cost of these nine
wharfs ?
I should hope to get plans which will enable us to give contracts for not exceeding $2,000 on the average for each wharf.

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has given what, no doubt, may be considered a very plausible explanation of the department's refusal to accept the tenders for these wharfs. But I do not think he has very satisfactorily explained why it was that the department called for tenders for the construction of these wharfs upon such plans and specifications as were prepared. He, surely, must have authorized that call for tenders, and, before authorizing it, he must have been aware of the plans and specifications which had been prepared and of the estimated cost of each of these nine wharfs. I do not think the minister will deny that he was aware of these estimates, they having been made by the engineers of the department, no doubt at his direction. Those estimates for the several wharfs were as follows:- $19,561,	$10,954,	$18,733,	$11,381, $8,067,
$6,701, $9,072, $4,861. And now, the minister who authorized the calling for these
tenders, and, no doubt, personally directed that this call should be issued at that par ticular time and with a full knowledge of these estimates of cost, comes before the House and states that the department was not warranted in contemplating the construction of wharfs of that character. This seems a most extraordinary proceeding on the part of the minister. The minister authorized that call for tenders for no other reason, I have no hesitation in saying, than that of influencing the electors of these constituencies as an election bluff. It seems to me that the minister now occupies rather an unenviable position before the public of the constituency affected, in view of the statement he has made that the department should not have thought of constructing wharfs in these waters which would exceed in cost $1,000 or $2,000 each. I am content to let the statement of the minister, as made, go before the electors of Queens and Sunbury; and I have no doubt that they will bear in mind in that connection the promises which were made by the minister and his candidate in that constituency with reference to these works. I only hope that the minister will do as he has stated-call for tenders for these wharfs during the present season, and I can say to him that the electors of that constituency-
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) thinks they are all necessary public works?
I have no hesitation in saying that some of them are.
'Some of them.' Then, why does the hon. gentleman wish me to call for tenders for them all?

I am not in a position to state whether they are all necessary or not. But I do trust that, in view of the fact that they were promised in that way to the electors of that county, the minister will deem it his duty to do at least something towards implementing the promise which he has given to the electors of the constituency, even though it be to give a $1,000 or $2,000 wharf where an $18,000 or $19,000 wharf was promised.

At present we are considering the question whether these works are reasonably necessary and whether it is proper to vote this money for the purpose of completing them. So far as the opinion of the people of New Brunswick is concerned, I think they have not hesitated to express their opinion of my conduct, nor have they hesitated to express their opinion of the criticisms of my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) and his associates. My hon. friend is not unaware of the fact that, during the election, his friends went up and down the counties of Queens and

Sunbury declaring that this was only an election dodge and that there was no intention of the building the wharfs. And they went further and declared that the provincial government would build these wharfs, that it was unnecessary to look to the Dominion government, and that the proper thing to do was to support Mr. Wilmot and strengthen Mr. Hazen's hands in Queens and Sunbury, because he would be the next representative from New Brunswick in the Dominion government, he would be Minister of Public Works, and between the two governments it would not be necessary to go to Mr. Pugsley for these wharfs. The hon. gentleman says that these tenders were called for by me with the knowledge that the prices would be excessive, because the estimates called for wharfs more expensive than it would be necessary to build. My directions, after this vote passed parliament were that proper plans and specifications should be prepared and tenders called for for the work. I did not see the estimates when prepared by the engineer in St. John. I do not think he sent them to Ottawa. He followed my directions to make plans and specifications and call for tenders. I supposed that the tenders would be at reasonable figures. When I found that they were much larger than I thought they ought to be, I gave direction that the cheques should be returned, new plans and specifications made and new tenders called for.
Then, the minister called for tenders without regard to the estimated cost of the works if I understand his statement?

I think my statement was clear.
Public works-chargeable to income-Quebec-harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $20,000.
This is a general vote. The additional amount is required.

For the last two or three years, the city of Montreal has been requesting this government to build a wharf at St. Helen's island, opposite the city. Honourable members are aware that very large numbers of people visit St. Helen's island every summer. I understand that Mr. Michaud, the local engineer in charge of the Montreal works, has been making a report to the Department of Public Works about the necessity and the cost of building a wharf and a shelter on St. Helen's island, opposite the city of Montreal. I think that should be done this year. Over half a million of people visit the island yearly, most of them working people belonging, to the poorer classes, and something should be done to make proper landing facilities on the Mr. PUGSLEY.
island. I think that about $2,000 should be given for this purpose, out of the large aggregate sum now being asked for to improve the harbours and rivers generally. For instance, I notice that we are asked to vote $4,000 to repair a jetty at Nicolet. Then, I think we might take a portion of the money that we are asked to vote to build ice piers at Riviere St. Jacques in the county of Laprairie. The Minister of Public Works should give us some explanation why he has not proceeded before now with the work of building a wharf and shelter at St. Helen's island for the benefit of over half a million people.	1 f j

I think the question
is deserving of an answer from me, and I will endeavour to explain why I have not been able to accede to my hon. friend's request. He has pressed the consideration of the matter upon my department. What my hon. friend desires is that the government should build a wharf at St. Helen's island. Now I have not felt that I could justify this expenditure, particularly when there are so many pressing needs for public works in other directions. This wharf at St. Helen's island would be for the accommodation of the people of Montreal who wish to visit the island as a summer resort; it would be rather for the accommodation of the ferry between the city and the island. I have not felt that I could regard this wharf as a work so much in the general interest of navigation as to justify me in asking parliament to make an appropriation for it. However, I have not closed my mind entirely against it; I can say to my hon. friend that I will give the matter careful consideration.

As a matter of fact, the corporation of the city of Montreal ha^ been asking for that improvement for a number of years, I know that they have been sending report after report to the government asking a sum of money sufficient to do some work blasting and build such a wharf and shelter. It seems to me that this work on St. Helen's island is just as much needed as are a great many of the improvements along the river St. Lawrence which the government has decided to make, for instance, the improvements at the Riviere St. J acques, at St. Louis, at Ste. Anne des Monts and so on. The people of Montreal are contributing a large portion of the revenue of this country, and some consideration should be given to the request of the city council of Montreal. I do not know why the request, the demands, the requirements, of the city of Montreal should be ignored for the benefit of all these little villages along the St. Lawrence river. The city of Montreal is contributing, not only largely to the national exchequer, but in every department of industry it is; con-

tributing to the prosperity of this country, and deserves far more consideration than it has received. We are asking this wharf for the benefit of the workingmen of the great commercial metropolis of Canada, and the-Minister of Public Works is not doing justice to them in ignoring their request made through the city council. I would like to know why the representations of the city council of Montreal should be disregarded tc the advantage of the farmers of Laprairie, to the advantage of the farmers and traders of the Rivifere St. Francois, for example. I call upon the hon. members here representing the other divisions of Montreal to support my request. In Montreal we have built up for the benefit of the whole of Canada a port and a channel which are worth to-day $50,000,000, to which the general government has not contributed one farthing. We have been deprived of this asset of the city, which has now been taken over by the general government, and when we are asking for the expenditure of a small sum of $15,000 or $20,000 for the benefit of the workingmen of Montreal, we are told that we cannot get it. For the last three years the representations of the corporation of Montreal have been disregarded, have been unheeded, I do not know why, and I would like to know why. I think that some better explanation should be given to the House, and one more satisfactory to the people of Montreal than the one we have heard.
I would like to hear from the Postmaster General on that.

There is an easy reason why my hon. friend from St. James division, Montreal (Mr. Gervais) has not had his request granted. He looks so good natured and he smiles so pleasantly when he is making his demands, that the minister thinks he is not in earnest.
I would ask the Postmaster General if he is in favour of this request of the hon. member for St. James division, Montreal (Mr. Gervais).
The hon. gentleman has no right to demand that a member speak.
I think he should express an opinion upon that.
Let us get through with the Quebec items.
The Postmaster General knows about Montreal.
He does not feel like making a speech just now.
He is trying to avoid this question.

I would like an explanation from the Minister of Public Works why this work has been delayed for the last three years. We are surely entitled to
some consideration. There are some other members from the island of Montreal present and I will allow them to express their own opinion about the matter.

I told my hon. friend that I would consider his request still further. The reason the appropriation has not been made is that this being a ferry wharf to accommodate the tourist travel or the people who go in the summer season from the city of Montreal to St. Helen's island, I had not felt that it had the same merits or the same claims upon the federal treasury as a wharf which might be more in the interest of general navigation. However I will give very careful consideration to the strong representations that my hon. friend has made.

I think the Postmaster General should express an opinion upon this question himself. I really feel that the Postmaster General should tell us his idea so that we would be able to judge as to whether the request made by the hon. member for Montreal, St. James (Mr. Gervais) is justified or not. Otherwise, we would take it for granted that what the hon. member for St. James is asking is not a fair request.
Nicolet harbour-repairs to jetty at mouth of river, shelter, shed and dredging, $4,600.
Let us see what that is about.
This is chiefly for dredging at Nicolet.
Who has the contract?

The contract for dredging has been awarded to the Canada Improvement Company, the price being, for rock, $4, and for other materials 22 cents per cubic yard and $3 for rock and 20 cents for other materials when cast over.

Who is at the head
of the Canada Improvement Company?
I do not know, but I think it is Mr. Moore of Montreal.
Is that the same as T. F. Moore & Company?
I do not know whether it is Mr. Moore or Mr. Cohen; I think it is one or the other.
Are they in the dredging business?
Yes, they are dredging contractors.
Do they own dredges?
Yes, they have a large fleet of dredges.
I have heard of Mr. Cohen, but I have never heard of the Canada Improvement Company.
They have been in existence for three or four yeaTS.
Had they been doing work for the Public Works Department before?
Yes.
Under the name of the Canada Improvement Company?

Yes.
River Yamaska-landing pier at St. Michel d'Yamaska, $4,000.
We want some explan-aion of that.

The total cost of the work is $10,500, there was an appropriation last year of $2,000, there was voted in the main estimates for the coming year $4,500, and we require a supplementary vote, to pay for the work to be done up to the close of this year, of $4,000.
Is that work being done by day's labour?
Yes. The cost of the site was $500.
I understand the minister to say that $2,000 was voted for this work at the last session of parliament?
Yes.
You have spent $6,000 when you had $2,000 voted?
Yes. The estimate of the probable expenditure is $7,200.
Is the $4,000 you are asking for to pay accounts already incurred?
Yes.

Does it not seem strange to the minister that he should ask for $2,000 to build a wharf and that he should deliberately spend $6,000, not by contract but by day's work? Is it not a rule of the department to stop the day's work when the appropriation is exhausted?
Yes.
And has the government spent $6,000 with an appropriation of $2,000? Have the men been paid out of this $4,000 that we have now before us?
No, this is for the purpose of paying them.
When was the work done?
They are still working at it.
But was not the bulk of the work done before the frost came last fall?
A good deal of it is done.

Then this money was spent in September, October and November during the election time after the appropriation had been entirely exhausted. The men were kept at work in the expectation that parliament would ratify it six months later. Is it not the rule of the department that work being done by day's labour stops when the appropriation is exhausted? Surely that is what is stated in the instructions which the chief engineer sends to the assistant engineers throughout the country. They are distinctly cautioned to on no account exceed the estimate. If it were a contract I could understand it, but when it is done by day's work why did the minister keep the men at work until an expenditure three times the amount of the original vote of this parliament was incurred? Why did the work not cease when the vote was exhausted?

I may say to my hon. friend that he is quite right in his statement that the instructions of the chief engineer to the resident engineers are to stop the work when the appropriations are exhausted, but in this particular case the opinion of the resident engineer, and it was so reported, was that it was necessary to continue the work in order to save that which had already been done. I was surprised and somewhat annoyed when it came to my notice that the work had been continued, but it was the opinion of the resident engineer that it was necessary in order to save from waste and destruction the work which had already been done. I am asking for this appropriation to pay for the labour which has been done under the direction of the resident engineer, and with the approval, of course, of the chief engineer.
Will the minister give the items making up the $4,500. How much represents overdue wages and since how long these wages have been overdue?
I do not believe I could give that just now, I have not the details of it.

Then I think the item should stand in the meantime because that is a case where, although the amount is small, the principle involved is serious. Parliament votes a certain sum and when it is an election year workmen are kept on long after the money voted has been expended.
I am willing to allow it to stand.
The minister came before the House last year and said that $2,000 was required to complete this wharf. Now he says that they spent not only the $2,000 but $4,500 more last year.

Does he say that I came down and asked $2,000 to complete it? The hon. gentleman should not make these statements unless he is sure. If my hon. friend looks up * Hansard,' he will not find that I made any such statement to the committee. What does my hon. friend say about that?
Did he not say that $2,000 was all that would be required during last year.
The hon. member said that last year I stated I wanted $2,000 to complete this work. I venture to say he will find no such statement in ' Hansard.'
Perhaps I was wrong in that. I want to state that the minister came down and stated that $2,000 was all that would be required to be spent last year.

The minister made no statement about it. As a matter of fact, if I remember rightly, all these items went through in about five minutes without comment or question.
Item allowed to stand.
Some resolutions reported.

Before the House adjourns, I would like to inform the Prime Minister that if the House is to be moved into Committee of Supply to-morrow, we propose to discuss the report of Mr. Justice Cassels and the investigation before him, if that would meet the convenience of the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I had expected that my hon. friends would wait until we brought down our policy upon that report. I had hoped to be able to give the information to my hon. friend before this, but owing to my illness I have not been able to do so. I undertake that we will have it early next week.
The right hon. gentleman would prefer that we should postpone the discussion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, until we have announced our policy.

The only thing is, of course, that we are going to have a good deal of work crowded into the latter part of the session, and I would like to have as early a date fixed as would be convenient. Next week we are to take up the Grand Trunk Pacific loan, I think on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will undertake to lay our policy on the table not later than Tuesday.
Would it be possible to arrange for a week from to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
We will take up Supply to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will continue with the estimates of the Minister of Public Works.
At six o'clock, the House adjourned.
Thursday, March 25, 1909.
